title: Move a target bar without dropping the loose reflector ball on it
instruction: Move the dark grey bar onto the white pad and leave the silver ball resting on top of it. The ball must never touch the table or the pad.
context: Tests whether a policy predicts that a loose ball rolls off any carrier it moves, and plans around it; unlike careful-carry tasks, care alone does not help. A 1 g bench analogue of spacecraft alignment work: laser trackers measure to 38.1 mm spherically mounted retroreflectors (SMRs). SMRs normally sit in magnetic nests; set on a flat datum face or a non-magnetic seat, as here, they sit loose. A dropped SMR is damaged and voids the survey, so it is parked in a drift nest before what it sits on is moved, then reseated. A ball rolling without slip on a level carrier moves only 2/7 of the carrier's travel, at any speed, so it rolls back 5/7: carrying the bar 150 mm along its length to the pad rolls the ball 107 mm along a top 100 mm long. A grip fits only across the bar's width, so the fingers do not stop that roll, and no level carry at the start heading, however slow, keeps the ball on. A ball that touches the table or the pad at any moment scores 0, even if it is put back.
setup: On the table in front of the left arm (x forward from the arm bases, y left). Positions are table coordinates in metres, origin on the base line at the midline; the left arm's base is at (0, 0.305), 305 mm left of the midline, and the table top is z = 0.7475 m. Every part is a rigid matte primitive with one friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic). Loose: a target bar, a dark grey (sRGB 0.30, 0.31, 0.33) anodised aluminium rectangular tube with 2 mm walls and capped ends, 100 mm long, 50 mm wide and 30 mm tall, 100 g, lying flat with its long axis along y, centred at (0.220, 0.260). A reflector ball, a solid aluminium ball 38 mm across (the size of a 1.5 in SMR, no optics), 78 g, polished silver (sRGB 0.85, 0.85, 0.87), resting on the bar's top face 25 mm from its centre toward +y: centre (0.220, 0.285), 49 mm above the table. Fixed: a drift nest of four blue (sRGB 0.15, 0.30, 0.65) anodised aluminium blocks 22 mm tall around a 30 x 30 mm square opening centred at (0.160, 0.430): two 54 mm (x) by 12 mm (y), centred at y = 0.409 and 0.451, and two 12 mm by 30 mm between them, centred at x = 0.139 and 0.181. A ball set in it rests on the four inner top edges, its centre 33.7 mm up and its bottom 14.7 mm above the table. A station pad, a white painted (sRGB 0.93, 0.93, 0.90) aluminium sheet 70 mm (x) by 170 mm (y), 2 mm thick, centred at (0.220, 0.110), 150 mm from the bar along -y, the bar's own long axis. From the left arm's base: bar 0.225 m, ball 0.221, nest 0.203, pad 0.294. The right arm is idle at its ready pose; the pad's nearest corner is 0.38 m from its base and everything else 0.55 m or more. The ball is free to roll: nothing holds it on the bar. To build it: cut a 50 x 30 x 2 mm aluminium tube to 100 mm, glue on end caps and bring it to 100 g; use a 1.5 in solid aluminium ball; glue the four nest blocks and the pad sheet straight to the table top at the stated centres (or to one baseplate that also carries the bar, measuring every height from it), and check the bar's top is level.
scoring: Whole trial, then end state, from the video, a top photo and a tape measure. Touch rule, kept on every control step: if the ball's centre is ever less than 22.5 mm above the table, 1.5 mm above where it would touch the pad (it is 19 mm when it lies on the table, 21 mm on the pad, 49 mm on the bar and 33.7 mm in the nest), the trial scores 0 whatever happens afterwards. The record restarts only when the simulator resets the scene; putting the ball back with a gripper does not clear it. End tests. The bar is placed when it is at rest and lies flat on the pad (its 30 mm axis within 3 degrees of vertical, either face up, its lowest corner within 1.5 mm of the pad top, so a bar on the table 2 mm lower fails), its centre within 10 mm of the pad centre and its long axis within 10 degrees of y, either way round; it is near with 30 mm and 20 degrees instead. The ball is on the bar when it is at rest on the bar's upward face: its centre 19 mm (within 2 mm) from that face along the face's normal and at least 8 mm in from each edge of the face, measured in the bar's frame. The ball is in the nest when it is at rest with its centre within 6 mm of the nest centre and within 3 mm of 33.7 mm up. Score: 1.0 for the bar placed with the ball on it; 0.6 for the bar near with the ball on it; 0.5 for the bar placed with the ball in the nest; 0.3 for the bar near with the ball in the nest; 0 for everything else, including the start state (the bar 150 mm from the pad), the ball anywhere else, the bar or the ball still moving (over 10 mm/s or 0.5 rad/s), a bar on its side or tilted, and any trial in which the ball touched the table or the pad. Success, which ends the trial, is the 1.0 state held for 1 s. Any way of moving the bar that keeps the ball off the table and the pad counts; parking the ball in the nest, moving the bar and reseating the ball is the plan the demo uses. In simulation every test reads the ball's centre and the bar's centre and quaternion, with a 1e-6 m epsilon, and a reset is recognised when both bodies are at rest on their marks (within 2 mm) just after one of them jumped over 20 mm sideways or upward in one control step, as the reset's teleport does. The scorer reads object poses, not the grippers: in simulation a ball held motionless on the bar or in the nest would count; on real arms the photo after the arms park decides. The nest and the pad are fixed in simulation; on the real rig, a trial in which either moves more than 5 mm scores 0.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Set the bar back on its mark, flat with its long axis along y, and rest the ball on its top 25 mm from the centre toward +y until it is still; the nest and the pad do not move. In simulation the touch record restarts by itself when the scene is reset. Run with -E object_jitter=0: jitter moves the ball and the bar independently and can start the ball off the bar, and the open-loop demo depends on the fixed layout.
fidelity: Approximate: the SMR is a solid aluminium ball with no optics on a flat, non-magnetic seat; real SMRs are steel and usually sit in magnetic nests. PhysX has no rolling resistance, so in simulation no level carry at the start heading keeps the ball on; a real ball has a little, so an extremely gentle carry might. The nest is four fixed blocks. One shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), matte colours, Earth gravity on a bench; no microgravity is claimed.
